problem:
Which of the following could be matrices of quadratic forms defined on ${R}^{4}?$

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 5 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}],\,E=[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}],\,F=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 2 & 5 & 4 & -1 \\ 3 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 6 & -1 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

feedback.problem:
Which of the following could be matrices of quadratic forms defined on ${R}^{2}?$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 7 \\ -2 & 1 & -1 \\ 7 & -1 & 9\end{aligned}],\,R=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that every quadratic form defined on ${R}^{2}$ has an associated $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine each matrix in turn.

- $P$ could be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on ${R}^{2}$ since it is a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix.

- $Q$ *cannot* be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on ${R}^{2}$ since it's a $3\times 3$ matrix (not $2\times 2$).

- $R$ *cannot* be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on ${R}^{2}.$ Although it's a $2\times 2$ matrix, $R$ is not symmetric since ${r}_{12}\ne {r}_{21}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$P$ only."
